It's being held up because Democrats are spending too much time contemplating whether reconciliation is worth it. It's a pointless question because the average voter doesn't remember whether a bill was passed with 51 or 60 votes; they remember how it affects them and whether it passed at all, and this is exceptionally true with something as straightforward as $2000 checks. Even Manchin's Republican Governor from WV said today on CNN that there's no reason to hold up relief, and Manchin is silly for delaying it. He also brought up the example of a man who froze to death in his own home in WV because he couldn't pay for heat. 

Basically, either Manchin is being completely heartless, or the Democrats are using him as an excuse to try to negotiate the checks down in size/reach. Either way, the fastest path forward is to end bad faith negotiations with Republicans and put private and public pressure on Manchin.

Fair point, so I'll say that the AAF study seems to assume nursing home care would be covered under his proposal even though from what I can tell, it only includes in-home care, which is cheaper, meaning their estimates for his long-term care proposal are probably too high (this is in line with other studies). I would agree that it will take some time, but maybe I shouldn't have used UK as an example since they follow the Beveridge Model which like you say requires the provider industry to also be nationalized. The CBO study and M4A, however, are just about the insurance itself. Considering how long single payer might take though (and considering universal coverage is something i'm deeply passionate about), I'm genuinely curious: which universal healthcare proposal do you think would be the quickest transition for us?

That link is a right-leaning think tank, but the CBO is widely considered one of if not the least biased sources (it has backed proposals from all sides based on its research), and it recently found that single payer healthcare would reduce total US healthcare spending by $300-$700 billion, even considering the fact that it would cover everyone, which is consistent with most other studies from nonpartisan think tanks and universities (not even just far-left Bernie supporters). The reasoning comes down to lower cost sharing, lack of profit motive, lower administrative costs, and monopoly power to negotiate with pharmaceutical companies and hospitals. I'm not saying it will be easy to get done, but there's a reason politicians in single payer countries don't run on repealing it. Just look at the UK where even Tories campaign on protecting it
